summary: With Passover near and an order out for His arrest, Jesus comes to Bethany six days before the feast, to the village where He raised Lazarus.
key_insight: John sets two sentences side by side. The leaders ordered anyone who knew where Jesus was to report it, and then Jesus came to Bethany, less than two miles from the city. He was not slipping in unnoticed; He came to the very place whose miracle had sealed their plot.
story: Since the council had decided to put Him to death, Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews. After a stay at Ephraim, a town near the wilderness, He was making His way back toward Jerusalem.

Now the Passover of the Jews was near. Many people went up from the country to Jerusalem ahead of the feast, to purify themselves. They looked for Jesus, and as they stood in the temple they talked it over. “What do you think,” they asked one another, “that He will not come to the feast?”
They had reason to wonder. The chief priests and the Pharisees had given a command that if anyone knew where He was, he should report it, so that they might seize Him.
Then, six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, the man who had been dead and whom He had raised from the dead.

scene.label: Purified for the feast
scene.text: No one who was ceremonially unclean could eat the Passover (Numbers 9:6–10). Uncleanness from contact with a dead body lasted seven days and needed sprinkling on the third and seventh days (Numbers 19:11–12). So pilgrims came up early. At Jesus’ trial the leaders would stay outside Pilate’s headquarters “lest they should be defiled” before the feast (John 18:28).

scene.label: A wanted man
scene.text: The order of John 11:57 turned every pilgrim and temple worker into a possible informer. It also explains why Judas’s offer later mattered so much to the chief priests: he could tell them where to find Jesus away from the crowds (Luke 22:6).

scene.label: From Ephraim to Bethany
scene.text: John last placed Jesus at Ephraim, on the edge of the wilderness north of Jerusalem (11:54). John does not trace His route from there. This timeline fills the gap from the other Gospels, as McGarvey does: Jesus went north along the border of Samaria and Galilee (Luke 17:11), crossed to the region beyond the Jordan (Mark 10:1), and came up to the city by way of Jericho with the pilgrims (Mark 10:46).

scene.label: Arriving before the Sabbath
scene.text: Six days before Passover most likely points to a Friday arrival. Travel on the Sabbath was limited to a short distance (compare Acts 1:12), so Jesus would have reached Bethany before sunset. John then dates the supper there and, “the next day,” the entry into Jerusalem (12:12).

witnesses.john: Only John tells of the pilgrims in the temple wondering whether Jesus would come, and of the order to report Him. John has marked the Passovers of Jesus’ ministry; now he begins to count days, and his story slows down. Eight of his twenty-one chapters (12–19) cover this last week, and John alone lets us date its beginning.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is not a fugitive caught in other men’s plans. With an arrest order posted, He comes toward Jerusalem at the time He has chosen, as He had said: “No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of Myself” (John 10:18).
seeing.living: The pilgrims in the temple talked about Jesus, guessed about Him and waited to see what He would do. Meanwhile He was already on His way, walking toward the danger for their sake. Do not stay among the spectators who discuss Him from a distance; He has come near enough to be found.
seeing.ponder: Are you still standing in the crowd wondering about Jesus, when He has already come close to you at great cost?

preaching.big_idea: With a warrant out for His arrest, Jesus came anyway, because His hour had come.
preaching.watch_for: Read 11:57 and 12:1 together: the arrest order, and then Jesus’ arrival. John also names Bethany by its miracle, “where Lazarus was who had been dead.” The sign that sealed the plot (11:47–53) becomes the setting for the last week.

title: Jesus Arrives at Bethany
